_note: Movement, drawn as a sequence of waypoints the archaeology reaches in order. A route is a line through dated sites, NOT a measured path: nobody walked a straight line, and a route drawn 1.8 million years long is a summary of a process that took tens of thousands of years. `overWater` marks a crossing that required boats or a land bridge that no longer exists. `c` says how well the sequence is supported.

routes.label: Out of Africa, the first time — about 1.8 million years ago
routes.note: East Africa to the Caucasus, then east along the southern edge of Asia. This is the dispersal that put hominins in Georgia, India and Java before the genus Homo had a big brain by modern standards.

routes.label: North into China — Sunda to the Loess Plateau
routes.note: A northern branch of the same dispersal, reaching Yunnan by 1.7 million years ago and the Zhoukoudian cave system, near Beijing, by 780,000.

routes.label: Java — the longest occupation in this record
routes.note: Hominins reach Java early and stay for over a million and a half years. Nothing else on this map holds one region for that long.

routes.label: The first Europeans — Levant to northern Spain
routes.note: The oldest well-dated European hominins are at Atapuerca, in northern Spain, by about 900,000 years ago. They arrived from the east, along the Mediterranean.

routes.label: The edge of the boreal zone — Britain at 900,000 years
routes.note: Happisburgh, in Norfolk, shows hominins on the coast of what is now England when Britain was still joined to the continent. It is the coldest place in this record.

routes.label: The Neanderthal range — Iberia to the Altai
routes.note: From the Atlantic to southern Siberia, roughly 8,000 kilometres. The whole population that held it was probably never more than a few tens of thousands of people.

routes.label: The Denisovan range — Altai to the Tibetan plateau, and further
routes.note: The fossils run from Denisova Cave to a single jaw at 3,280 metres on the Tibetan plateau. The dashed end of this line is not excavated: it exists because Oceanian genomes need a source that got that far.

routes.label: Inside Africa — the structure that came before the exit
routes.note: Our origin is not one valley. Fossils of the same evolving population are found at Morocco at 315,000 years, Ethiopia at 233,000, and South Africa at 100,000, and stone-tool cultures change together across the whole continent.

routes.label: The first exit that failed
routes.note: Modern humans reach the Levant by about 180,000 years ago — Misliya Cave, then Skhul and Qafzeh — and are then absent from the region's fossil record for tens of thousands of years. Whether this dispersal left any descendants is unresolved.

routes.label: Out of Africa — the dispersal that worked, from about 70,000 years ago
routes.note: Across the Red Sea into Arabia, then east along the coast of Asia. This is the movement that produced every living population outside Africa, and it happened while sea level was far lower than today.

routes.label: The Sahul crossing — at least 20 open-water passages
routes.note: Sunda and Sahul were never joined even at the lowest sea level: reaching Australia and New Guinea needed watercraft. Madjedbebe's 65,000-year date is disputed — the floor of 50,000 is not.

routes.label: Across the continent — the oldest continuous occupation
routes.note: Within a few thousand years of landing, people are at Devil's Lair in the south-west and at Lake Mungo in the south-east, where the oldest known cremation in the world was found.

routes.label: West, into Europe — arriving about 45,000 years ago
routes.note: The earliest modern human sites in Europe — Bacho Kiro in Bulgaria, then Oase in Romania, Zlatý kůň in Bohemia, then Britain. In every case they arrived to a continent Neanderthals were still living on.

routes.label: East, into Siberia
routes.note: Ust'-Ishim, on the Irtysh river in western Siberia, is 45,000 years old, and Kostenki and Sunghir sit on the Don. People were living at these latitudes through the coldest part of the last ice age.

routes.label: Beringia — the standstill, and then the Americas
routes.note: At the last glacial maximum the sea was about 120 metres lower and Siberia was joined to Alaska by dry land. The genetics suggest a pause of several thousand years there before the move south — a standstill, not a corridor.

routes.label: To Luzon — a sea crossing nobody expected
routes.note: Callao Cave on Luzon has hominin remains at 67,000 years, and getting there meant crossing open water. The line is drawn for the dated occupation only, because that is what the evidence dates — the ancestors who made the crossing did it far earlier, and no trace of the journey survives.

routes.label: To Flores — over deep water, 700,000 years ago
routes.note: Flores has never been joined to the mainland. Something crossed the strait, and by 700,000 years ago its descendants at Mata Menge were already small. That is the oldest evidence of watercraft anywhere in this record — 600,000 years before modern humans did it.

routes.label: The East Asian Middle Pleistocene form
routes.note: Dali, Jinniushan, Xuchang and Harbin form a group of large-brained, large-faced people in China in the Middle Pleistocene. Whether they are one species, several, or part of the Neanderthal–Denisovan stem is not agreed.
